title: Reading a crochet chart
subtitle: How to follow a symbol diagram from the right row and in the right direction
excerpt: A crochet chart maps each stitch to a position using symbols. Learn to read the grid, follow the row direction, and cross-reference the stitch key.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small graphic that stands for one specific crochet stitch, placed on the chart where that stitch sits in the finished piece.
The legend at the side or bottom of a crochet chart that names each symbol and the stitch it represents.
A horizontal line of symbols on a crochet chart, read from right to left on odd rows and left to right on even rows for flat crochet.

content.text: A crochet chart is a diagram that shows each stitch as a
chart symbol
. You use one alongside or instead of a written pattern. Charts work well for lace and motif patterns, where a picture of the stitch layout is easier to follow than a list of abbreviations.
The symbol key
Every chart comes with a
symbol key
. Read the key before reading the chart. Find the symbol for each stitch you know: chain, slip stitch, double crochet, treble. Patterns that use specialist stitches add those to the key as well.

Standard international symbols are widely shared. A chain is an oval; a slip stitch is a filled oval or a small filled circle; a double crochet (UK) is an X or a plus sign; a treble (UK) has one crossbar on a tall vertical. Most pattern sources use these, but always check the key for the specific chart you are using.
Reading direction
The direction you read a
chart row
depends on whether the piece is worked flat or in the round.
Flat crochet: odd-numbered rows read right to left; even-numbered rows read left to right. This mirrors the way you turn the work at the end of each row.
In-the-round: every round reads from right to left (or anticlockwise), because you never turn the work.
Charts often print an arrow or a number at the row start to confirm the direction. When in doubt, follow the arrow.
How to follow a chart step by step
Read the key end-to-end before working any stitches.
Find row 1 on the chart. It is usually at the bottom. Confirm the reading direction from the arrow or row number.
Work each symbol from right to left (or in the stated direction), placing a stitch marker after the last stitch of the row.
Tick or highlight the completed row on a printed copy so you always know which row comes next.
Compare your work against the chart after every few rows. The shape of the stitches in your fabric should match the shape of the symbol cluster on the chart.
Common problems

items.symptom: The stitch count does not match after a row
items.cause: You read a row in the wrong direction, which means the turning chain was placed at the wrong end.
items.fix: Count back to find where the row count diverged and recount the symbols from the correct starting side.

items.symptom: A symbol in the chart does not appear in the key
items.cause: The chart uses a non-standard symbol, or the key is on a different page.
items.fix: Check all pages of the pattern for a full key. If none exists, the symbol likely represents the most common stitch in the pattern, which the designer omitted from the key. Compare to a standard symbol reference.

items.symptom: The motif shape in your work looks nothing like the chart
items.cause: The work is being read right to left when it should read left to right, or the tension is very different from the pattern's stated gauge.
items.fix: Re-read the direction notes for that chart and confirm you are on the correct row. Then check your gauge against the pattern's recommendation.

content.text: What to try next

Once you can follow a simple chart, try a granny square chart. The round-based grid is compact, the symbol set is small (chain, treble, slip stitch), and each round is self-contained. Granny square charts appear on the pattern cards in the Motifs section.
